title: Tenant routing & isolation playbook — Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a working playbook for platform engineers and SREs. Goal: codify routing policies, isolation boundaries, and control-plane responsibilities across the three deployment modes (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Use it for design reviews, implementation checklists, and runbook inputs.

Quick summary (one-liner):
- Hosted: multi-tenant control plane + shared public data-plane pools, strong logical isolation (auth/quotas, mTLS, per-tenant routing) but weaker network isolation.
- Dedicated: tenant gets reserved pools (GPU+hosts) with predictable throughput; control plane still multi-tenant but with stricter routing rules and capacity reservations.
- Private: full customer-managed data plane, optional private control plane; network isolation and tenant routing enforced by customer VPC/peering.

Design goals / constraints:
- Preserve latency SLOs while enabling cost-efficient multiplexing (batching/cache) where safe.
- Fail-open model: degrade to cheaper model variant or region rather than returning 5xx for client-facing features.
- Clear isolation boundaries for compliance customers (must support tenancy-level auditability and encryption-in-flight and at-rest).
- Minimal blast radius for noisy tenants.

Terminology (short):
- Control plane: configuration, model catalog, token billing, routing policy decisions, rollout manager.
- Data plane: actual inference pods/servers that handle token generation/embeddings.
- Tenant routing key: primary identifier used to route (api-key, customer-id header).
- Instance pool: a set of GPUs/nodes colocated and optimized for certain model families.

Routing policy primitives we use: (policy pseudo-DSL)
- match(tenant, region, model_tag, cost_tier) -> route to pool A/B/C
- fallback(order: same_region_variant, cross_region_variant, low_cost_variant)
- isolation_level: logical | reserved | dedicated | private-network
- enforce_network_policy(boolean)

Hosted (notes and trade-offs):
- Typical customer: PLG, low compliance needs, wants low friction.
- Data plane: shared public pools; routing uses tenant id -> routing table -> pool. Pools tagged by model capability, quantization profile, hw-type.
- Isolation: logical only. Per-tenant namespaces at runtime (process-level or container-level). KV cache is tenant-scoped. Persistent data (KV snapshots, logs) are tagged by tenant id.
- Network model: TLS termination at edge (load balancers) controlled by Redwood. Internal connections mTLS. No customer VPC.
- Failure modes: noisy-tenant can cause queueing pressure; mitigate with per-tenant concurrency & token rate limits, dynamic throttling and QoS reservations for high-tier tenants.
- Routing specifics: controller decides pool via capacity-aware bin-packing algorithm. If pool overloaded, policy triggers fallback to compatible model (smaller quantized or next-best).
- Ops: easier to roll out new kernel optimizations and cross-tenant batching improvements.

Dedicated (notes and trade-offs):
- Typical customer: enterprise wanting predictable throughput and data isolation without running infra.
- Data plane: pools reserved for tenant (single-tenant pool per model-class or shared across small number of tenant’s workloads if configured). These are pre-allocated (committed capacity).
- Isolation: tenant gets reserved compute; network isolation is stronger (private subnets, firewalls), but control plane might still be multi-tenant. Storage may be logically isolated or optional dedicated volumes.
- Routing specifics: routing table maps tenant -> reserved pool(s). Autoscaler is scoped to tenant pool(s) with minimums set by contract. For overflow, policy must decide between queueing, bursting to shared overflow pools (if customer allows), or cross-tenant fallback (usually disallowed by high-compliance customers).
- Failure modes: under-provisioned commit causes higher latencies; mitigation: pre-configured burst capacity or SLA-backed cross-region fallback.
- Networking: in-hosted-managed Dedicated, we support private subnets and restricted ACLs; edge TLS termination remains with Redwood unless Private mode requested.

Private (notes and trade-offs):
- Typical customer: regulated, on-prem, or VPC-only deployments.
- Data plane: customer-managed, can be air-gapped. Control plane: optional customer-managed control-plane; in hybrid we provide a thin control API over secure channel.
- Isolation: full network isolation as determined by customer. Routing is generally configured and enforced by customer network (VPC routing tables, ingress controllers).
- Routing specifics: Redwood control plane issues signed routing policies to the customer control endpoint (pull model). Tenant routing may be entirely local to customer infra (recommended).
- Failure modes: limited Redwood visibility makes automatic fallbacks harder. We recommend tactical fallbacks implemented locally in customer's infra.

Cross-cutting concerns (applies to all modes):
- AuthN/AuthZ: API key -> tenant verification at edge. Keys stored in KMS; control plane generates short-lived mTLS creds to talk to data plane.
- Auditing: every request must carry tenant id and traced across control/data plane for audit logs. Hosted/Dedicated: logs collected centrally; Private: either ship logs to Redwood via secure channel or keep local retention.
- Billing & metering: token counts aggregated per-tenant at proxy edge. For Dedicated we reconcile edge counters with pool counters to detect drift.
- SLO routing rules: prefer same-region pools if added latency of cross-region exceeds token-SLO slack (parametrized).

Concrete routing patterns and examples:
1) Low-latency customer in Hosted: prefer same-region small-quant model in pool-A. Policy: match(tenantX, region=us-west-2, model_tag=gptx-8b) -> pool-A; fallback to pool-B (quantized) then to pool-C (cross-region).
2) Dedicated reserved pool with burst to overflow: tenantY has reserved pool-Y with min=4 GPUs. If queue depth > 300ms latency threshold AND burst_quota_remaining > 0 -> route to shared-overflow pool (if customer opt-in).
3) Private (pull control plane): customer infra subscribes to control-plane to receive policy bundle. Local ingress matches header X-Customer-Tenant and uses local routing table.

Implementation checklist (actionable):
- [ ] Define policy DSL canonical schema and JSON schema (api-plat RFC-2026)
- [ ] Implement per-tenant QoS tokens and circuit-breakers in edge proxy (envoy filter?)
- [ ] Ensure mTLS short-lived cert rotation between control and data planes (weekly default)
- [ ] Add control-plane UI to show active routing decisions + why-fallback (for ops)
- [ ] Add experiments telemetry: which fallback was used, cost delta, latency impact

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Shared overflow for Dedicated: do we permit by default or require explicit opt-in? (security vs cost) — proposer: Rafael.
- How aggressive should cross-region fallbacks be for Hosted? We need a latency budget model per-customer.
- For Private hybrid (Redwood-managed control plane + customer data plane), what minimal telemetry must be shipped to Redwood for safety while satisfying compliance?

Runbook snippets (for SREs):
- Detecting noisy tenant in Hosted: alert when single-tenant token usage > 30% of pool CPU for 5m AND queue latency > 95th percentile SLO. Action: apply temporary per-tenant concurrency cap, notify customer, move to reserved pool if repeat offender.
- Dedicated latency breach: if pool utilization > 90% for >10m -> if burst allowed, route to overflow; otherwise open incident for capacity increase and enable steady degradation to cached responses.

Notes-to-self / TODOs (fragments):
- gather perf numbers for cross-region penalty (us-west -> eu-west) for 8k tokens across model families.
- check legal for log forwarding requirements for EU customers in Private mode.
- sync with product on default opt-in for overflow; need pricing appendix.

References / links (internal):
- infra PR with initial routing controller: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/481
- prior doc: CONFLUENCE-PLAT/tenant-routing-arch
- related ticket: JIRA-PLAT-8672

Bottom line: routing and isolation are a sliding scale. The control plane should be policy-driven and expressive enough to capture tenancy, latency, cost, and compliance constraints. Implementation will require tight collaboration between edge, control-plane, and SRE to ensure predictable behavior and observable fallbacks.

Author notes: keep this doc light — move finalized design into Confluence after decisions on overflow and telemetry are locked.
